name: Isthmus-Pajapan Nahuatl
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.source_named: Garcia de Leon, Antonio. 1976. Pajapan: un dialecto mexicano del Golfo (INAH); also Ando, Koji. 2007. Gramatica nahuatl de Pajapan (no online copy found)

new_statements.quote: El acento recae por lo general en la penúltima sílaba. En nuestro material sólo lo hemos marcado cuando recae en otras sílabas. Lo hemos considerado fonémico porque establece cambios de significado: aya "todavía", ayá "ya no"; ga:wa "deja", gawáh "caballo". 2. Patrón silábico. [...] [verb morphology:] ... [el] acento se desplaza a la última sílaba. Ejemplo: goniskiáh "lo tomarían si pudieran".
new_statements.translation: Stress generally falls on the penultimate syllable. In our material we have marked it only when it falls on other syllables. We have considered it phonemic because it produces changes of meaning: aya 'still', ayá 'no longer'; ga:wa 'leave (it)', gawáh 'horse'. 2. Syllable pattern. [...] [verb morphology:] ... the stress shifts to the last syllable. Example: goniskiáh 'they would take it if they could'.
new_statements.citation: García de León, Antonio. 1976. Pajapan, un dialecto mexicano del Golfo. (Colección Científica 43, Lingüística.) México: SEP-INAH, Departamento de Lingüística.
new_statements.locator: Phonology chapter, paragraph on 'acento' immediately preceding '2. Patrón silábico'; exact page not shown by Google Books snippet view — Flores Farfán (1999) cites this phonology discussion as 'De León, 1976: 55 y ss.'. Stress-shift remark is in the verb-morphology section just before §32613.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is penultimate; a residue of words (some adverbs, loans like gawáh 'horse', and certain inflected verb forms where a suffix attracts/shifts stress to the final syllable) have final stress, which the author writes with an acute accent and treats as phonemically contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on word-level secondary stress in the snippets; at clause level the author says each clause has one primary accent and one or more secondary accents, the primary accent almost always on the last word of the clause ('El acento primario casi siempre recae en la última palabra...').
new_statements.exceptions: Minimal pairs aya/ayá, ga:wa/gawáh with final stress; stress shifts to the final syllable in certain verb forms (example goniskiáh 'lo tomarían si pudieran', tied to a verbal suffix discussed at §3261x). A 1984 SMA Mesa Redonda paper summarises: 'En Pajapan, es normalmente grave' (normally penultimate) while calling Nahua accent 'émico' in most dialects.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement from the phonology chapter (citation/lexical forms); separate clause-level statement places primary clause accent on the last word depending on final intonation contour.
new_statements.identity_note: García de León 1976 describes the speech of the municipio of Pajapan, Veracruz = Glottolog isth1241 / ISO nhp exactly (WALS 'Nahuatl (Pajapan)', code npa, is based on the same book). Do not substitute Wolgemuth's Mecayapan-Tatahuicapan grammar (isth1242, nhx), which only notes that Pajapan is 'muy parecido'. García de León's 1968 Tlalocan texts are from Zaragoza and Jáltipan, not Pajapan.
